title: How a computer understands code
sub: The CPU, the compiler and the .NET trick
cards/0/title: The CPU only understands machine code
cards/0/body:
The CPU is the computer's "brain". It can only do very simple things: add two numbers, compare them, jump to another instruction. These instructions are stored as numbers. That is machine code.

Writing in numbers is painful for people, so we write in programming languages such as C#:
cards/0/deep: A CPU's instruction set is called its ISA. x64 and ARM64 have different ones: the same operation is encoded with different bytes. That is why a native binary is always built for a specific architecture and OS.
cards/1/body: A program that turns source code into instructions for the machine is called a compiler.
cards/2/q: What can the CPU run directly?
cards/2/options/3: Only what was typed in Notepad
cards/2/explain: The CPU only understands its own machine code. Everything else has to be translated first.
cards/2/wrong/1: C# is text for people. The CPU can't read it, so it needs a translation.
cards/2/wrong/2: The CPU reads no programming language at all, only machine code.
cards/3/body:
Most Windows laptops have an x64 CPU. M-series MacBooks and phones use ARM. These are different "machine languages".

A program translated for x64 won't run on ARM. It's like a manual in Japanese handed to someone who only reads English.
cards/4/q: A game was compiled to x64 machine code and launched on a phone with an ARM CPU. What happens?
cards/4/explain: x64 machine code is made of instructions an ARM CPU simply doesn't know.
cards/4/wrong/2: Machine code doesn't translate itself. That takes special programs called emulators.
cards/5/title: The .NET trick: translate in two steps
cards/5/body:
First the compiler turns C# not into machine code but into an intermediate language called CIL. It is the same for every CPU.

Then, on the actual computer and at startup, CIL is translated into machine code for that exact CPU.

Think of sheet music: the composer writes it once, and it can be played on any instrument.
cards/5/deep: Java works in a similar way with JVM bytecode. The difference is that the CLR was designed from day one for many languages (C#, F#, VB.NET) with a shared type system, the CTS.
cards/6/title: Managed code: code with a supervisor
cards/6/body:
A program that runs inside .NET is called managed. It is launched and looked after by the CLR, the Common Language Runtime: it translates CIL into machine code, manages memory and catches errors.

Code that is compiled straight to machine code and runs on its own is called native.
cards/7/q: Match each term to its meaning
cards/7/pairs/2/1: Intermediate language shared by all CPUs
cards/8/q: Put the path of a .NET program in order
cards/8/items/1: The compiler translates it to CIL
cards/8/items/2: At startup, CIL is translated to machine code
cards/8/items/3: The CPU runs the machine code
cards/8/explain: These are the four steps from the Microsoft article: compiler, CIL, machine code, execution.
cards/9/q: Hello.dll was built on an x64 laptop and copied to an ARM Mac that has .NET installed. What happens?
cards/9/options/2: It runs only after a rebuild on the Mac
cards/9/explain: Hello.dll contains CIL, not machine code. The ARM machine code is produced right at startup.
cards/9/wrong/1: That would be true for a native program. But the .dll holds CIL, which works on any CPU.
